name: Yoga as the stilling of the mind's activities (citta-vṛtti-nirodha)

definitions.definition: Yoga is the stilling of the mind's activities (YS 1.2), after which the seer abides in its own form (1.3); Vyāsa equates yoga with samādhi and admits it only in the one-pointed and stilled mind (YBh 1.1); commentators describe stilling as the inward dissolution of the activities into their cause.

relations.note: stilling is achieved by these means

definitions.definition: The mind is a product of the guṇas (YBh 1.2), seen and not self-luminous (4.19), variegated by countless latent tendencies yet existing for another (4.24); it is one, has many objects and endures (YBh 1.32); it has seen properties (cognitions) and seven unseen ones — stilling, merit, impressions, transformation, life, movement, capacity (YBh 3.15); coloured by seer and seen it apprehends all (4.23). Commentators equate it with the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

name: The five activities of the mind (pañca vṛttayaḥ)

definitions.definition: The mind's activities are five — valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep and memory — each afflicted or unafflicted (YS 1.5–11); activities and impressions produce one another in a ceaseless wheel (YBh 1.5); all have the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion and are to be stilled (YBh 1.11).

Yoga accepts three means of valid cognition — perception, inference and testimony (YS 1.7) — defined in YBh 1.7; the insight of samādhi has the particular as object, beyond testimony and inference (1.49), and the perception of nirvitarkā samāpatti is the 'highest perception' (YBh 1.42).

For Yoga, sleep is itself an activity of the mind, whose support is the cognition of absence (YS 1.10) — a cognition because it is recollected on waking ('I slept happily', 'I slept heavily') — and it must be stilled in samādhi like other cognitions (YBh 1.10); the knowledge of dream or sleep may serve as a support for steadying the mind (1.38).

Activities leave impressions that produce activities again (YBh 1.5); impressions born of samādhi-insight obstruct others (1.50), and those of stilling obstruct even these (YBh 1.51); impressions of emergence and of stilling alternate in the transformation of stilling (3.9); direct perception of impressions gives knowledge of former births (3.18); memory and impressions are of one form (4.9).

relations.note: YBh 3.18: impressions that cause memory and afflictions are vāsanā; those that cause fruition are merit and demerit

definitions.definition: Latent tendencies, laid down by the experience of afflictions, karma and fruition, manifest only when suited to the ripening karma (4.8), stay connected across births, places and times (4.9), are beginningless because the will to be is eternal (4.10), and cease when their cause, result, substrate and support cease (4.11); the mind, though variegated by them, exists for another (4.24).

name: The seer and the seen (draṣṭṛ and dṛśya)

definitions.definition: Reality is divided into the seer — pure seeing, the puruṣa (2.20) — and the seen — the guṇas as elements and senses, for experience and liberation (2.18); their conjunction, caused by ignorance, is the cause of suffering (2.17, 2.24), and I-am-ness is their seeming identity (2.6).

The puruṣa is seeing alone, pure, yet conforming to cognitions (2.20); unchanging, it always knows the mind's activities (4.18); consciousness that does not pass over into objects (4.22); utterly unlike sattva (3.35); neither the same as the buddhi nor entirely different (YBh 2.20); pure, alone and liberated when established in itself (YBh 1.51). Knowledge of the puruṣa comes from saṃyama on what exists for itself (3.35).

The affliction of I-am-ness is the seeming identity of the power of seeing (buddhi) with the seer (2.6); in samprajñāta samādhi, asmitā is awareness of a single self (YBh 1.17); 'asmitā-mātra' is the sixth unparticularized principle (YBh 2.19) and the source of created minds (4.4); in the gaps of discernment the thoughts 'I am', 'mine' arise (YBh 4.27). Bhoja distinguishes asmitā (mere being shining in the inward-turned mind) from ahaṃkāra (apprehending objects as 'I') (RM 1.17).

The puruṣa is the witness (pratisaṃvedin) of the buddhi (YBh 2.17, 2.20); the mind's activities are always known to it (4.18); Vijñānabhikṣu explains its knowing through the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi (YV 1.7).

The seen has the nature of illumination, activity and inertia, consists of elements and senses, and exists for experience and liberation (2.18); the guṇas are called pradhāna (YBh 2.18); it is real and common to all puruṣas (2.22).

Sattva (illumination), rajas (activity) and tamas (inertia) (2.18) — mutually dependent, distinct in power, transforming; their conflicting activity makes everything suffering for the discerning (2.15); all things are arrangements of them (4.13); the mind has three guṇas and its states depend on their mix (YBh 1.2).

name: The four levels of the guṇas (guṇa-parvan)

definitions.definition: The guṇas exist at four levels: the particularized (sixteen: five elements, ten senses and mind), the unparticularized (five tanmātras and I-am-ness), the mere mark (mahat) and the unmarked (pradhāna) (2.19, YBh 2.19); subtlety of objects ends in the unmarked (1.45).

name: The seen exists for the seer (bhoga and apavarga)

definitions.definition: The seen exists for experience and liberation (2.18); its very being is for the seer's sake (2.21); the mind, acting in combination, exists for another (4.24); bondage is the buddhi's not completing the puruṣa's purpose, liberation its completion (YBh 2.18).

There are many puruṣas: the seen ceases for one whose purpose is accomplished but continues for others, being common to them (2.22, YBh 2.22); the end of saṃsāra holds for the skilled, not for others (YBh 4.33).

relations.note: each puruṣa is pure consciousness; plurality is of puruṣas, not of kinds of consciousness

name: The conjunction of seer and seen (saṃyoga)

definitions.definition: The beginningless conjunction of seer and seen is the cause of what is to be avoided (2.17); it is the cause of apprehending owner and owned (2.23); its cause is ignorance (2.24); its absence is kaivalya (2.25). Vyāsa records eight views on the 'non-seeing' that causes it (YBh 2.23).

The two means of stilling (1.12): practice is effort toward stability, grounded by long, uninterrupted, devoted cultivation (1.13–14); dispassion dams the stream toward objects while practice opens the stream of discrimination (YBh 1.12).

Lower dispassion is the consciousness of mastery of one free of thirst for seen and scriptural objects (1.15); higher dispassion is freedom from thirst for the guṇas, from discernment of the puruṣa — the utmost limit of knowledge, inseparable from kaivalya (1.16, YBh 1.16); dispassion even toward the highest powers yields kaivalya (3.50). Vācaspati divides the lower into four stages (see pth:vacaspati-four-stages-of-vairagya).

Īśvara is a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), the teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by the praṇava (1.27). He is ever free and ever Lord, his pre-eminence resting on excellent sattva, without equal or superior; his purpose is compassion for beings (YBh 1.24–25). Devotion to him brings samādhi near (1.23, 2.45); he favours the devotee by mere intention (YBh 1.23). He is not the material of the world. Vijñānabhikṣu makes knowledge of the Supreme Lord the swift cause of liberation (YV 1.51).

relations.note: differs from liberated puruṣas in never having been bound

definitions.definition: The praṇava designates Īśvara by a fixed, not conventional, relation, like a lamp and its light (1.27, YBh 1.27); its repetition with contemplation of its meaning makes the mind one-pointed (1.28, YBh 1.28) and removes obstacles (1.29).

name: The four attitudes (maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā)

definitions.definition: Friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous and equanimity toward the non-virtuous clarify the mind (1.33); cultivating them produces white dharma and steadiness (YBh 1.33); saṃyama on the first three yields strengths, but equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation (3.23, YBh 3.23); YBh 4.10 calls friendliness and the rest 'the abodes (vihāra) of meditators'.

relations.standpoint: as cultivations (bhāvanā) of four attitudes toward beings
relations.note: Same four names and 'vihāra' vocabulary as the Buddhist brahmavihāras (and the Jain four bhāvanās); but YS 1.33 assigns each to a class of object and aims at clarity of mind, and Vyāsa denies that upekṣā is a cultivation — the lists are not simply identical.

definitions.definition: In a mind whose activities have dwindled, like a flawless crystal, coalescence is resting on and taking the form of grasper, grasping or grasped (1.41); it is savitarkā (mixed with word, object and knowledge constructions), nirvitarkā (object alone), savicārā and nirvicārā (subtle objects) (1.42–44), extending to the unmarked (1.45); these four are samādhi with seed (1.46).

relations.note: Shared terms vitarka/vicāra and samāpatti with the Buddhist jhāna system; the structures differ (Yoga's pairs are defined by gross vs subtle objects and presence of constructions) — correspondence contested

definitions.definition: Samādhi accompanied by reasoning, reflection, bliss and I-am-ness (1.17): the first has all four, the second lacks reasoning, the third lacks reflection, the fourth is I-am-ness alone; all have a support (YBh 1.17); it occurs in the one-pointed mind (YBh 1.1). Commentators differ on the objects of the bliss and I-am-ness levels (Vācaspati, Bhoja RM 1.17, Vijñānabhikṣu YV 1.17).

The 'other' samādhi, preceded by practice of the cognition of cessation, with only impressions remaining (1.18); its means is higher dispassion; the mind becomes supportless, as if non-existent (YBh 1.18); nothing is cognized in it (YBh 1.2). Bhoja: reached by rejecting every arising activity 'not this, not this' (RM 1.18).

name: Samādhi with seed and seedless (sabīja, nirbīja)

definitions.definition: The four coalescences have an external thing as seed and are samādhi with seed (1.46); when even the impression of truth-bearing insight is stilled there is seedless samādhi (1.51); the three inner limbs are outer relative to it (3.8).

In the lucidity of nirvicārā coalescence there is inner clarity (1.47); insight there is truth-bearing (1.48), with the particular as its object unlike testimony and inference (1.49); its impression obstructs other impressions (1.50). Vyāsa quotes: 'having climbed the clarity of insight, the wise one looks on the sorrowing as one on a mountain looks on those below' (YBh 1.47).

name: Samādhi from means and from birth (upāya-pratyaya, bhava-pratyaya)

definitions.definition: For the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti the state has becoming as its cause (1.19); for yogins it arises from means — faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight (1.20).

name: The bodiless and those merged in prakṛti

definitions.definition: Beings who experience a state 'like kaivalya' but return: the bodiless (gods, per Vyāsa) pass through the ripening of their impressions; those merged in prakṛti remain until the mind returns by force of its unfinished task (YBh 1.19); they are placed outside the worlds, 'in the state of liberation' (YBh 3.26). Bhoja identifies the bodiless with those who rest content in the bliss-samādhi and the prakṛtilayas with those content in the I-am-ness samādhi (RM 1.17).

Yogins are of nine kinds — mild, middling or intense in means, each with mild, middling or intense ardor; for the intensely ardent samādhi is near, and nearest for the intense in means and ardor (1.21–22, YBh 1.20–22).

name: The five means: faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight

definitions.definition: The means by which samādhi arises for yogins (1.20): faith (serenity of mind, protecting like a mother), from which energy, from which mindfulness, with which the mind is concentrated, to which discerning insight comes; from its practice and dispassion, asamprajñāta (YBh 1.20).

relations.standpoint: as a list of five qualities leading to samādhi and insight
relations.note: Same five names as the Buddhist indriya/bala (saddhā, viriya, sati, samādhi, paññā); Vyāsa gives them as a causal sequence ending in asamprajñāta samādhi.

definitions.definition: Austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.1), for cultivating samādhi and thinning the afflictions (2.2); taught for the unconcentrated mind; austerity must not disturb the mind (YBh 2.1).

Ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion and clinging to life (2.3) — the five errors (YBh 2.3), called tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra and andhatāmisra (YBh 1.8); ignorance is their field (2.4); they are the root of the karmic residue (2.12); gross forms are removed by meditation, subtle ones by involution (2.10–11); they cease through the cloud of dharma (4.30).

The afflictions may be dormant, thinned, interrupted or active (2.4); Vyāsa adds a fifth, 'burnt-seed' state, found only in one whose afflictions are exhausted, 'skilled' and in his last body (YBh 2.4).

Rooted in the afflictions, the karmic residue ripens in this or a future birth (2.12); while the root remains it ripens as birth, life-span and experience (2.13); the mass accumulated in a life, manifested at death, produces one birth (YBh 2.13); merit only removes obstruction, like a farmer opening a dyke (4.3).

name: The fruition of karma: birth, life-span, experience

definitions.definition: Karma ripens as the kind of birth, the length of life and experience (2.13), bearing joy or anguish according to merit or demerit (2.14).

Black (of the wicked), white-and-black (through external means that help and harm others), white (of those given to austerity, self-study and meditation), and neither white nor black — the yogin's, of renunciants whose afflictions are exhausted (4.7, YBh 4.7).

name: Everything is suffering for the discerning

definitions.definition: Because of the sufferings of change, anguish and impressions, and the conflict of the guṇas, everything is suffering for the discerning (2.15); the yogin is sensitive to it like an eyeball (YBh 2.15); even the happiness of contentment is suffering compared with kaivalya (YBh 3.18).

name: The fourfold scheme of the śāstra (heya, heya-hetu, hāna, hānopāya)

definitions.definition: As medicine has four parts — disease, its cause, health, remedy — so the śāstra has four: saṃsāra (what is to be avoided, future suffering), its cause (the conjunction of seer and seen), liberation (avoidance, the absence of conjunction) and its means (right seeing, unwavering discernment) (YBh 2.15; YS 2.16–26).

The cognition of the difference between sattva and puruṣa (YBh 2.26); unwavering, it is the means of liberation (2.26); limbs of yoga make knowledge shine up to it (2.28); from it come sovereignty and omniscience (3.49); complete, it yields the cloud of dharma (4.29); the discerning mind bends toward kaivalya (4.26).

name: The sevenfold final insight (saptadhā prāntabhūmi prajñā)

definitions.definition: The discerning one's insight at the final stage is sevenfold (2.27): four releases regarding what is to be done (known, exhausted, realized, cultivated) and three releases of the mind (buddhi's task done; guṇas dissolving; the puruṣa alone) (YBh 2.27).

Restraints, observances, posture, breath-regulation, sense-withdrawal, concentration, meditation and samādhi (2.29); their practice destroys impurity until discriminative discernment (2.28); the last three are inner limbs (3.7). Nārāyaṇatīrtha subsumes many named yogas under the eight limbs.
Non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy and non-possessiveness (2.30); universal and unlimited they are the great vow (2.31); non-harming is their root (YBh 2.30).
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.32, YBh 2.32).

When harmful thoughts oppress, cultivate their opposites (2.33): reflect that violence and the rest, done, caused or approved, from greed, anger or delusion, have endless suffering and ignorance as fruit (2.34, YBh 2.33–34).

name: Signs of establishment in the restraints and observances

definitions.definition: Established in non-harming, hostility ceases nearby; in truth, actions and fruits rest on one's word; in non-stealing, jewels come; in celibacy, vigour; in non-possessiveness, knowledge of births (2.35–39); purity, contentment, austerity, self-study and devotion yield their fruits (2.40–45). Vyāsa calls these 'powers' (YBh 2.39).

Concentration, meditation and samādhi on one object (3.4); from its mastery the light of insight (3.5); applied by stages, 'yoga itself being the teacher' (3.6, YBh 3.6); applied to various objects it yields the powers.
The last three limbs are inner compared with the first five (3.7), but outer compared with seedless samādhi (3.8).

name: The three transformations of the mind

definitions.definition: Stilling (impressions of stilling overpower those of emergence, 3.9, with a peaceful flow, 3.10), samādhi (all-objectness dwindles, one-pointedness rises, 3.11) and one-pointedness (subsiding and arising cognitions alike, 3.12).

name: Transformation of property, time-mark and state

definitions.definition: What holds for the mind holds for the elements and senses: transformation of property (dharma), of time-mark (lakṣaṇa: future, present, past) and of state (avasthā) (3.13, YBh 3.13); difference of sequence explains difference of transformation (3.15).

The property-bearer conforms to properties past, present and not yet determinable (3.14); since everything has the nature of everything, without an enduring continuant there could be no experience or memory (YBh 3.14).

The moment is time at its utmost minuteness and alone real; sequence is the flow of moments; hours and days are constructions of the buddhi (YBh 3.52); sequence is apprehended at the end of a transformation (4.33); saṃyama on moment and sequence gives discriminative knowledge (3.52). Permanence is twofold: unchanging (puruṣa) and changing (guṇas) (YBh 4.33).

name: Past and future exist in their own form

definitions.definition: Past and future exist in their own form because properties differ in their time-paths (4.12); otherwise knowledge of them would be objectless and action for future fruit pointless (YBh 4.12); manifest or subtle, they are guṇas (4.13).

name: The object does not depend on one mind

definitions.definition: A thing is common to many minds and stands on its own (4.14–16): the same thing produces pleasure, pain, delusion or indifference in different minds (YBh 4.15); if it depended on one mind, what would it be when that mind was distracted? (4.16); it is known or unknown as it colours the mind (4.17). Vyāsa rejects those who say the object is only a construction of cognition, like a dream (YBh 4.14), and those who say 'all is mind only' (YBh 4.23).

The mind is not self-illuminating because it is seen (4.19); it cannot know itself and its object at one time (4.20); if seen by another mind there would be infinite regress and confusion of memories (4.21); awareness of one's own cognition arises when unmoving consciousness takes its form (4.22).

Saṃyama on particular objects yields powers: knowledge of past and future, of the cries of beings, of former births, of other minds; invisibility; knowledge of death; strengths; knowledge of the worlds, stars, the body; freedom from hunger; steadiness; sight of siddhas; intuition; knowledge of the mind and of the puruṣa; divine senses; entering another body; levitation and departure at death; radiance; divine hearing; movement through space; mastery of elements and senses; the eight powers; omnipotence and omniscience (3.16–49).
Powers arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (4.1, YBh 4.1); only the mind born of meditation is without residue (4.6).

The powers are obstacles in samādhi and powers only in emergence (3.37); kaivalya comes from dispassion even toward the highest (3.50); invited by the celestials, the yogin should form neither attachment nor pride (3.51, YBh 3.51); kaivalya does not require the powers (YBh 3.55).

name: The eight lordly powers (aṇimā and the rest)

definitions.definition: Minuteness, lightness, greatness, reach, irresistible will, control, lordship and settling things at will — arising from mastery of the elements, with perfection and invulnerability of the body; though able, the yogin does not overturn the order set by the earlier-perfected Lord (3.45, YBh 3.45).

Minds created from I-am-ness alone (4.4), all directed by one mind (4.5); of the five kinds (by the five sources), only the meditation-born is without residue (4.6, YBh 4.6); the first knower taught Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25).

For one without self-interest even in the highest reflection, complete discernment brings the samādhi called cloud of dharma (4.29); from it afflictions and karma cease (4.30), knowledge becomes infinite (4.31) and the guṇas complete their sequence (4.32). Vyāsa also names the pure mind's meditation 'dharmamegha' (YBh 1.2).

The absence of the conjunction of seer and seen (2.25); arising when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity (3.55) and from dispassion even toward the highest power (3.50); the return of the guṇas, their purpose fulfilled, to their source, or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34). Vyāsa: then the puruṣa is the light of its own form alone, stainless, alone (YBh 2.27, 3.55).

Vyāsa: with the cloud of dharma the afflictions are uprooted and karmic residues destroyed; 'when afflictions and karma cease, the wise one is liberated while living', since error is the cause of becoming (YBh 4.30); one whose afflictions are exhausted has no karma for a future birth (YBh 2.12) and is 'in his last body' (YBh 2.4).

name: The five levels of the mind (citta-bhūmi)

definitions.definition: Scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed and stilled (YBh 1.1); samādhi in the distracted mind is not yoga; samprajñāta occurs in the one-pointed, asamprajñāta in the stilled mind.

The beginner (prāthamakalpika), the honey-stage yogin (madhubhūmika) with truth-bearing insight, the one whose insight is light (prajñājyotis) who has mastered elements and senses, and the one beyond what is to be cultivated (atikrāntabhāvanīya) whose aim is the mind's dissolution (YBh 3.51).

name: The five vital airs in Yoga

definitions.definition: Life is the joint activity of the senses, fivefold: prāṇa (mouth and nose to the heart), samāna (to the navel), apāna (down to the soles), udāna (up to the head) and vyāna (pervading); prāṇa is chief (YBh 3.39); mastery of udāna and samāna yields powers (3.39–40).

name: Bodily loci of concentration and saṃyama

definitions.definition: Places for binding the mind: the navel wheel, the heart-lotus, the light in the head, the tips of nose and tongue (YBh 3.1); the throat-well, the tortoise channel in the chest (3.30–31); the heart, 'the small lotus-house in the city of Brahman' (3.34); on the navel wheel one knows the three humours and seven constituents (YBh 3.29).

Seven worlds from the Avīci hell to the world of Brahmā (bhūr, the intermediate world, Mahendra's heaven, Prajāpati's mahar, and Brahmā's jana, tapas and satya), with hells and seven netherworlds below, the earth of seven continents around Meru, and classes of gods whose highest members enjoy the meditations with reasoning, reflection, bliss and I-am-ness; the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti are outside the worlds (YBh 3.26). Known by saṃyama on the sun (3.26–28).

Word, object and cognition are confused through mutual superimposition; saṃyama on their distinction gives knowledge of the cries of all beings (3.17). The word is a single unit grasped by the buddhi from the letters (YBh 3.17); the relation of word and meaning is held eternal (YBh 1.27); savitarkā coalescence is mixed with these constructions (1.42).

name: Death in Yoga: clinging, omens, departure

definitions.definition: Clinging to life (abhiniveśa), a fear of death found even in the newborn worm, shows past births (2.9, YBh 2.9); karma ripening as life-span is fast or slow, and saṃyama on it or omens give knowledge of death — omens personal, from other beings and from the gods (3.22, YBh 3.22); mastery of udāna gives departure at will at death (3.39); the mass of karma manifested at death forms the next birth (YBh 2.13).

name: Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha and the transmission of Yoga

definitions.definition: Īśvara is the teacher even of the ancients (1.26); the first knower out of compassion taught the doctrine to Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25). Commentators read 'anuśāsana' (1.1) as Patañjali's re-teaching of yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and give the lineage Pitāmaha — Śeṣa (Patañjali) — Vyāsa — Vācaspati and Vijñānabhikṣu. In the stages of saṃyama 'yoga itself is the teacher' (YBh 3.6).

In Īśvara the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25); for one with only discernment of sattva and puruṣa there is knowledge of all (3.49); discriminative knowledge is all-embracing and without sequence (3.54); when coverings are gone knowledge is infinite and what remains to be known is little (4.31).
